Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
At fifty-three, David had spent the better part of two decades navigating the complex caseloads of a county social services office. His life shifted abruptly five years ago, during a walk home past a dimly lit municipal underpass. The attack was sudden and violent. He was forced into a narrow, windowless maintenance closet, the heavy door shutting with a final, metallic click that severed him from the world outside. He remembers the suffocating weight of the confined dark, the cold concrete against his back, and the terrifying suspension of time. He did not know how long he remained there, nor could he predict when the door would open. When the man finally released him and David stumbled into the alley, the ordinary streets around him felt irrevocably compromised. In the months that followed, David’s internal landscape became a series of uncharted territories. When memories of the underpass surfaced, they did not arrive as organized accounts. He knew precisely what had transpired, yet the words consistently dissolved in his throat, leaving a hollow, inarticulate terror that rose in his chest with a force that stole his breath. Alongside that terror sat a heavy, hot shame that coated him long after the images faded. When the images returned, he also began pushing them out of his mind, gripping his steering wheel until his knuckles blanched, telling himself that if he simply refused to dwell on the past, the pressure would ease. But the space he tried to clear was never empty. It was occupied by a quiet, relentless rumination on revenge, a mental script he ran while folding his wife’s laundry or waiting for the coffee maker to finish, turning over every imagined scenario where he finally made the assailant pay for what was taken from him. David’s daily environment became a landscape of calibrated risks. As a social worker, his role required moving through unfamiliar neighborhoods and entering small, private offices to conduct intake assessments. He came to believe that unfamiliarity was synonymous with vulnerability. He began tracing the same three blocks to the clinic, memorizing sightlines and exits before stepping out of his car. In his own vehicle, he developed the habit of checking behind him before entering the building, his hand lingering on the door handle, scanning the street for shadows or unfamiliar vehicles. When a case file required a longer wait than anticipated, or a client was late to an appointment, his stomach tightened; he was certain that delays meant something bad had already begun. The clinic’s windowless consultation room became untenable. The four walls felt like the maintenance closet returning. He began rescheduling clients to the bright, open staff lounge, explaining it was for better accessibility, though he knew it was because he needed to see the doors and the windows. Over time, these habits calcified into a rigid routine. He lost a supervisory position to a younger caseworker who willingly navigated new territory and sat quietly in closed offices. At home, his wife noticed he flinched when she approached him after he’d been staring out the window, his body rigid with the same terror he felt when the elevator hesitated between floors. He stopped suggesting new restaurants or routes, sticking only to places where the layout felt predictable. What finally brought David to my office was a Tuesday morning when he sat in his car for twenty minutes, unable to cross the bridge to the clinic because the morning traffic had stalled. He felt a profound exhaustion, a quiet realization that the man who attacked him five years ago still dictated his routines. He was hoping for a way to stop scanning the rearview mirror and to find words that did not taste like ash, but what frightened him most was the certainty that the fear had already become the only reliable thing he had left.
